extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates or beginning graduate students studying functional analysis (Hilbert and Banach spaces)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and results about Hilbert and Banach spaces: structure of bounded linear operators, geometry of Hilbert spaces (orthogonality, projections, orthonormal bases), dual-space identifications, adjoint operators, and Hahn–Banach extension/separation theorems. Intended to teach definitions, characterizations, and proofs of fundamental facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space of bounded linear operators is a normed linear space
rubrics_metrics.description: The set of bounded linear operators from X to Y, equipped with the operator norm, is a normed linear space (denoted L(X,Y)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scalar multiplication and addition are defined pointwise: (L1+L2)(x)=L1(x)+L2(x), (cL)(x)=cL(x). The operator norm satisfies the usual inequalities showing boundedness of sums and scalar multiples; explicit inequalities and norm estimates are given in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of L(X,Y) when Y is complete (Proposition 12.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X and Y are normed linear spaces and Y is complete, then the normed linear space L(X,Y) (bounded linear operators from X to Y) is a Banach space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: show Cauchy sequence of operators converges pointwise on X to a linear operator L, then use uniform boundedness/Cauchy estimates and completeness of Y to show limit operator is bounded and operator norms converge. Useful when constructing operator limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual space X* and its norm
rubrics_metrics.description: When Y is the scalar field F, bounded linear operators are linear functionals and the space F1 is complete; the space X* of bounded linear functionals (the dual) is a Banach space. Norm of x* in X* is kx*k = sup_{||x||≤1} |x*(x)|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a concrete way to compute norms of functionals; X* is always complete by Proposition 12.1 and the special-case remark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples/identifications of dual spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Several standard dual-space identifications and hypotheses that accompany them (e.g., L^p duals require σ-finiteness when p>1, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete examples given: (1) (L^p(S,µ))* ≅ L^{p'}(S,µ) for 1<p<∞ with p' the dual index (requires σ-finiteness in some statements); (2) (ℓ^p)* ≅ ℓ^{p'} for 1<p<∞; (3) C(S)* ≅ M(S) (regular Borel measures) when S compact Hausdorff; (4) (c0)* ≅ ℓ^1 and (ℓ^∞_n)* ≅ ℓ^1_n in finite-dimensional cases. Remarks note when hypotheses (σ-finiteness, p>1) cannot be dropped and references to the Riesz Representation Theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Hilbert space
rubrics_metrics.description: A Hilbert space is a complete normed linear space whose norm arises from an inner product: ||u|| = (u,u)^{1/2}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Euclidean spaces R^n, C^n, and L^2 spaces. Much of the section studies geometric consequences of this inner product structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schwarz (Cauchy–Schwarz) inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: For all u,v in a Hilbert space H, |(u,v)| ≤ ||u|| ||v||.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly to show continuity of the inner product, to derive triangle inequality and other norm inequalities. Text derives further estimates from Schwarz.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallelogram law and characterization of Hilbert spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Hilbert spaces satisfy the parallelogram law: ||u+v||^2 + ||u−v||^2 = 2||u||^2 + 2||v||^2. Conversely, a Banach space is a Hilbert space if its norm satisfies the parallelogram law (Jordan–von Neumann).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polarization identity uses this to recover the inner product from the norm; exercises/problems referenced for the converse proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polarization identity
rubrics_metrics.description: An identity expressing the inner product in terms of the norm: (u,v) = (1/4)∑_{k=0}^{3} i^k ||u + i^k v||^2 in the complex case (real case sum over {0,1}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to define the inner product from the norm in the Jordan–von Neumann converse and to relate norm and inner-product formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of best approximation / nearest point in closed convex (sub)sets (Lemma 12.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If M is a closed vector subspace (or even a closed convex set) of H and u ∈ H, then there exists v ∈ M with ||u−v|| = inf_{w∈M} ||u−w||.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key lemma for projection theorem; proof uses completeness and parallelogram law and constructs a minimizing sequence which is Cauchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthogonal complement M⊥
rubrics_metrics.description: For subset M⊂H, M⊥ = {u ∈ H : (u,v)=0 for all v∈M}. M⊥ is a closed vector subspace; M⊥ = {0} when M is dense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important for decompositions and projection; text notes that M⊥ is most interesting when M is closed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection theorem / orthogonal decomposition (Proposition 12.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If M is a closed vector subspace of H, then every u ∈ H decomposes uniquely as u = v + w with v ∈ M and w ∈ M⊥ (i.e., H = M ⊕ M⊥).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniqueness follows from M∩M⊥={0}; existence builds on Lemma 12.2 selecting v achieving the distance and showing u−v ∈ M⊥. Essential condition: M must be closed (counterexample: polynomials in L^2[0,1] are dense so nonclosed M gives M⊥={0} and no decomposition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Double orthogonal complement equality for closed subspaces (Corollary 12.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If M is a closed vector subspace of H then M⊥⊥ = M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows by applying the projection theorem to determine membership in M from orthogonality properties; remark ties to uniqueness in orthogonal decomposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riesz Representation Theorem for Hilbert spaces (Theorem 12.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every continuous linear functional ` on a Hilbert space H can be represented as `(u) = (u,v) for a unique v ∈ H, and ||`|| = ||v||.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses kernel M = {u : `(u)=0}, projection theorem to find a nonzero w ∈ M⊥, and constructs v as scalar multiple of w. Remarks compare this form to the L^p Riesz theorem and note canonical conjugate-linearity/isometry distinctions in abstract Hilbert spaces versus L^2 with complex conjugation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthonormal sets and Gram–Schmidt (definitions and algorithm remarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: An orthonormal set S ⊂ H has each vector of norm 1 and pairwise orthogonal. Gram–Schmidt converts finite linearly independent sets into orthonormal sets spanning the same subspace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: exponentials e^{inx} in L^2, Legendre polynomials normalized, Bessel-function-derived systems. Gram–Schmidt referenced as exercise/problem for algorithmic construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence of orthonormal series and square-summability criterion (Lemma 12.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If {u_j} is orthonormal in H, then the series ∑ c_j u_j converges iff ∑ |c_j|^2 < ∞, and when it converges the sum is independent of the order of terms. Norm identity: ||∑ c_j u_j||^2 = ∑ |c_j|^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Pythagorean identities for partial sums and completeness of H to pass to limits; rearrangement independence follows from absolute-sum-of-nonnegatives arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthogonal projection via orthonormal set and Bessel's inequality (Proposition 12.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an orthonormal set S and its closed span M, the orthogonal projection E on M is given by E(u) = ∑_{v∈S} (u,v) v (only countably many nonzero terms). Moreover ||E(u)||^2 = ∑ |(u,v)|^2 ≤ ||u||^2 (Bessel's inequality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convergence independent of order; partial-sum estimates give continuity and projection properties. Useful to compute projections and expansions in terms of orthonormal systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterizations of orthonormal bases and Parseval's equality (Corollary 12.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: For orthonormal S⊂H, the following are equivalent: (a) S is maximal orthonormal set, (b) E(u)=∑ (u,vα)vα for all u (S spans H in closure), (c) ||u||^2 = ∑ |(u,vα)|^2 for all u (Parseval), (d) polarization form of (c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology: maximal orthonormal set = orthonormal basis (not necessarily finite linear-algebra basis); Parseval/Parseval's equality equates norm squared with sum of squared coefficients. In L^2 context this formalizes Fourier series expansions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product basis for L^2 spaces (Proposition 12.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If L^2(X,µ) and L^2(Y,ν) each have countable orthonormal bases {u_i} and {v_j}, then {u_i(x)v_j(y)} is an orthonormal basis for L^2(X×Y, µ×ν).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: show orthonormality and maximality by testing orthogonality of an L^2 function w(x,y) against all basis products and using Fubini-style integrations to deduce w=0. Useful for building bases of product spaces (e.g., separable L^2 spaces).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension to orthonormal bases (Proposition 12.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any orthonormal set in a closed vector subspace M of H can be extended to an orthonormal basis of M (use Zorn's Lemma); hence every closed subspace has an orthonormal basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard maximality argument: order all orthonormal subsets by inclusion, take Zorn-maximal set S and apply Corollary 12.8 to see S spans M.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cardinality invariance of orthonormal bases (Proposition 12.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any two orthonormal bases of a Hilbert space have the same cardinality (the Hilbert-space dimension).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof constructs equivalence classes via chains of nonzero inner products between bases and shows a bijection class-by-class; remarks caution that additional structure on practical Hilbert spaces may not be preserved by arbitrary Hilbert-space isomorphisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operator norm characterization via inner products
rubrics_metrics.description: For a bounded linear operator L on H, ||L|| = sup_{||u||≤1,||v||≤1} |(L(u),v)|. Equivalently, ||L|| = sup_{||u||≤1} ||L(u)||.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: apply Schwarz inequality and choose v parallel to L(u) to attain equality in the sup. This formulation motivates thinking of (u,v)↦(L(u),v) as a matrix-like kernel for operators on H.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjoint operator existence and properties (Proposition 12.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: For bounded linear L:H→H there exists a unique (conjugate-linear) bounded operator L* such that (L*(u),v) = (u, L(v)) for all u,v in H. Moreover ||L*|| = ||L||.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: for fixed u, the map v↦(L(v),u) is a bounded linear functional; apply Riesz representation to obtain L*(u). Notes: L* is conjugate-linear in u, composition satisfies (L M)* = M* L*, and self-adjointness L*=L is an important class (e.g., orthogonal projections E satisfy E*=E).

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebra of bounded operators and adjoint relations
rubrics_metrics.description: B(H,H), the space of bounded operators on H, is closed under composition; norms satisfy submultiplicativity ||L M|| ≤ ||L|| ||M||; adjoint respects composition: (L M)* = M* L*.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These facts allow operator-theoretic algebraic manipulations and give Banach-algebra-like structure to B(H).

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthogonal projection properties (example)
rubrics_metrics.description: The orthogonal projection E onto closed subspace M is bounded with ||E|| = 1, self-adjoint (E* = E), and satisfies E^2 = E and E is identity on M and zero on M⊥.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pythagorean theorem gives ||E(u)|| ≤ ||u|| and equality holds on M; (1−E) is projection onto M⊥. Useful canonical example of a self-adjoint operator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hahn–Banach extension theorem (Theorem 12.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Y is a vector subspace of a normed linear space X and y* is a continuous linear functional on Y, then there exists a continuous linear functional x* on X extending y* with ||x*|| = ||y*||.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fundamental theorem guarantees abundance of continuous linear functionals and is used to characterize closed subspaces by functionals that vanish on them. The complex-case proof reduces to the real-case by extension of Re(y*).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hahn–Banach lemma for sublinear p (Lemma 12.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given real vector space X and sublinear function p with p(x+x') ≤ p(x)+p(x') and p(t x) = t p(x) for t≥0, any linear f on subspace Y dominated by p (f(y) ≤ p(y)) extends to linear F on X with F(x) ≤ p(x) for all x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Zorn's Lemma extending dominated linear functionals and an explicit construction on one-dimensional extension to maintain domination by p. This lemma is the core tool for the norm-preserving Hahn–Banach extension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation/Norming functional for point vs closed subspace (Corollary 12.15)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Y is a closed subspace of X and x0 ∉ Y, there exists x* ∈ X* with x*(y)=0 for all y∈Y and x*(x0)=1. Moreover ||x*|| can be taken to be 1/dist(x0,Y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct linear functional on span{Y,x0} with prescribed values and norm estimate, then extend by Hahn–Banach. Useful geometric separation result: closed subspaces are kernels of continuous linear functionals and points can be separated by functionals.
